paragraphs: I've worked in and around Lafayette for a long time, and properties like 490 St. Marys Road genuinely stand out  -  a gated, creek-side estate on nearly 1.5 acres with no visible neighbors and a kitchen that earns its own reaction is not something you encounter every week in this market. When I saw the listing come off market without a sale, it caught my attention in a different way, and that's why I'm writing.

Thirty-one days on market isn't a disaster, but for a home with this much going for it  -  the setting, the craftsmanship, the privacy, the sheer scale of the lot  -  it signals that the listing strategy didn't fully close the distance between what the property actually offers and what buyers were able to feel from the outside. At $891 per square foot, the number is supportable, but only if the marketing does the work of building that case for buyers before they make the drive. From what I can see, that case wasn't fully made.

I've put together a packet that walks through what I think happened, why the fundamentals here are still strong, and how I'd approach a relaunch differently. It's specific to this property, not a generic playbook.

If you're already working with a real estate professional toward a new listing, please feel free to disregard this entirely, no hard feelings. If you're not, I'd welcome a short conversation whenever the timing is right for you.

cover.tagline: The Blueprint for a Successful Sale

exec_summary.headline: A Gated Creek-Side Estate with Custom Craftsmanship  -  and a Listing That Didn't Show It
exec_summary.p1: 490 St. Marys Road has the kind of combination that serious Lafayette buyers actively search for and rarely find together: a nearly 1.5-acre gated lot with a seasonal creek running through it, a 3,144-square-foot home built with contractor-grade materials and artistic custom detail, a kitchen significant enough to generate its own reaction, and a setting private enough that no neighboring structures are visible from the property. The 3-car garage with wood doors, the dual-entry gated driveway, and the wildlife-corridor setting along Las Trampas Creek are genuine differentiators in a market where most premium inventory sits on conventional suburban lots. These are the features that justify a premium price point, and they are real.
exec_summary.p2: The listing history tells a different story. At $2,800,000 and $891 per square foot, this home sits at the high end of the Lafayette premium tier, which is a defensible position given what the property offers. But 31 days on market without a sale, on a home this distinctive, suggests that buyers encountered the number before they fully understood what the number was buying them. The listing description gestured at the features  -  'WOW kitchen,' 'postcard views,' 'artistic flair'  -  without giving buyers the visual depth and narrative specificity to feel confident at this price. The strategy described the home in outline. It never handed buyers the reasons to believe.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch for this property needs to accomplish one specific thing: close the gap between what buyers see on a screen and what they would feel walking this land. The setting, the privacy, the creek, the craftsmanship  -  none of that translates through flat photography and a paragraph with exclamation points. The right buyer for this home exists. Getting there requires media and a narrative built to match the property.

forensics.title: Friction #1: The Visual Story of This Setting Was Never Told
forensics.body: A gated 1.5-acre estate with a seasonal creek, no visible neighbors, and a dual-entry driveway is not something a standard front-elevation photo can explain. Buyers scrolling at $2,800,000 need to feel the scale and privacy of this property before they will invest the time to schedule a showing. The listing description used words like 'paradise' and 'postcard view,' but the visual record never showed buyers what those phrases meant in practice. At this price point, buyers are comparing carefully, and a property that can't be understood from the screen gets passed over in favor of one that can. The setting here is the premium. It needed to be the centerpiece of the visual campaign, not background context.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's Sky Tour captures the lot position, creek corridor, gated entry, and surrounding privacy from the air in a way ground photography simply cannot, giving buyers the spatial context that justifies the price before they ever set foot on the property.

forensics.title: Friction #2: A Premium Price Point With No Supporting Narrative
forensics.body: At $891 per square foot, this home sits at the top of the Lafayette premium tier, which the property can support. But buyers comparing options at this level are analytical. They want to understand specifically what they are getting at that number that they cannot find in a $750-per-square-foot alternative. The listing offered impressions  -  'finest materials,' 'expert workmanship,' 'masterpiece'  -  without translating those impressions into concrete, specific proof. A kitchen that earns a 'WOW' reaction needs more than the word 'WOW' in the description. The custom features, the material quality, the contractor-built details  -  all of it needed to be named and shown with enough precision that buyers could build their own case for the number. Without that, $891 per square foot reads as an ask, not a conclusion.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's Zillow Showcase placement pairs premium portal visibility with a narrative built the way a great buyer's agent would describe the home  -  specific, grounded in features, and structured to give buyers the rationale to arrive at the price with confidence, not skepticism.

forensics.title: Friction #3: Out-of-Area Buyers Who Were Never Reached
forensics.body: A property priced at $2,800,000 in Lafayette draws from a specific buyer profile: SF and East Bay professionals who are ready to trade urban density for land, privacy, and something they genuinely cannot find in the city. These buyers research extensively online before they will consider driving to Lamorinda, and they need to encounter this property while they are actively in that research phase. A standard MLS distribution waits for buyers to find the listing. It does not go find them. The buyers most likely to pay full price for a creek-side gated estate with this level of privacy were probably not browsing the MLS in May  -  they were browsing neighborhood lifestyle content and targeted searches well before that. The distribution strategy needed to be built for where those buyers actually spend their attention.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's geo-targeted digital campaigns place this property directly in front of SF and East Bay buyers who are actively researching Lamorinda, reaching them at the point of consideration  -  before they've found what they're looking for  -  rather than waiting for them to find the MLS.

positioning_table.verdict: At $891/sqft versus a benchmark range of $850-$920/sqft, this home sits in the middle of that range. At $891 per square foot, this home is positioned near the middle of the Lafayette premium tier  -  a placement the property's lot size, privacy, custom construction, and creek-front setting can genuinely support. The gap between what the numbers say and what the listing accomplished is not a pricing problem. It is a marketing problem. The assets that make this home worth the number were never shown with enough specificity or visual depth for buyers to arrive at the price with confidence.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Showing the Land, Not Just the House
pillars.body: Most buyers for a property like this will decide whether to schedule a showing based on what they can feel from the digital experience. A 1.5-acre gated creek-front estate with this level of privacy requires media that communicates scale, setting, and character  -  not just rooms. BrightWork's Sky Tour and Matterport 3D walk-through together give buyers the spatial and architectural depth to understand exactly what they are considering, from anywhere, before they make the drive. More informed buyers produce fewer wasted showings and stronger, more confident offers.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Building the Case for $891 Per Square Foot
pillars.body: At the top of the Lafayette premium tier, the marketing has to do specific work. Every custom feature  -  the kitchen, the garage, the materials, the setting  -  needs to be named, described with precision, and shown with photography that earns the number rather than just asserting it. BrightWork writes listing narratives the way a great buyer's agent describes a home to a serious client: specific, honest, and structured to give buyers a reason to believe before they schedule a showing. The goal is to make the price feel like a conclusion, not a demand.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Finding the Right Buyer, Not Waiting for Them
pillars.body: The buyer for a gated creek-side estate at $2,800,000 is a specific person, and they are not sitting on the MLS waiting for a new listing to appear. They are researching Lamorinda neighborhoods, privacy, land, and quality construction across multiple platforms before they ever contact an agent. BrightWork's geo-targeted digital campaigns and off-market private buyer list at offmarket.brightworkrealty.com put this property in front of those buyers during their research phase  -  not after they've already made other decisions. That is how a property like this finds the right buyer, rather than hoping the right buyer happens to find it.
